This measure, along with the Applicant's proposed rehabilitation of the construction yard (Subsection 4.2), could create a more diverse wildlife habitat, benefiting wildlife species which favor woodland openings but becoming less suitable for use by those species adapted to mature forest habitats.
The construction of the proposed project dams and reservoir would inundate about 2.3 miles of coldwater stream fishery habitat and associated riparian wildlife habitat. It is not expected that all populations of stream fauna or local populations of amphibians and reptiles within the proposed impoundment area would survive the effects of changing a stream environment to that of a reservoir. Trout residing in Bad Creek and West Bad Creek within the proposed impoundment area would probably be eliminated. Since the lower reservoir is already in existence, no further losses of stream habitat would be incurred.
Construction of the upper reservoir would lead to increased turbidity and sedimentation in Howard Creek and portions of Lake Jocassee. The adverse effects of these changes are unavoidable, although they could be mitigated as discussed earlier. Sedimentation of eroded solids could have a permanent adverse effect on the substrate of Howard Creek, depending upon the sediment transport capabilities of this stream after project construction. Changes in water quality could occur in the upper reservoir in comparison to that of the streams which would be impounded. Temperature alterations would also occur in the upper reservoir. Reduction in flow in Howard Creek would result from impoundment if flow augmentation is not provided.
Operation of the Bad Creek Project would result in fishery losses at Lake Jocassee due to entrainment and loss of coldwater habitat from pumping and generating. The magnitude of these losses is not known. Losses of coldwater habitat would also result from future increased operation of the Jocassee Pumped Storage Project and the Keowee Nuclear Plant (Section 3.2.2.3).
5.2.3 Recreation
Impoundment of water at the Bad Creek site would result in the loss of limited land and water-oriented recreation opportunities now available in the area, including hunting, fishing, primitive camping, sightseeing, hiking, and off-road motor vehicle use.
